*Translator's note:* Or “islands” (KJV, NIV, CEV); TEV “distant lands”; NLT “lands beyond the sea.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat) could be translated “judgment,” but here it seems to refer to the dispute or debate between the Lord and the nations.

*Study note:* The expression *this one from the east* refers to the Persian conqueror Cyrus, as later texts indicate (see {{Isaiah 44:28|44:28-45:6}}; {{Isaiah 46:11|46:11}}; {{Isaiah 48:14|48:14-16}}).

*Translator's note:* The interrogative particle is understood by ellipsis.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[in] righteousness called him to his foot.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he [the Lord] places before him [Cyrus] nations.”

*Translator's note:* The verb יַרְדְּ (yard) is an otherwise unattested Hiphil form from רָדָה (radah, “rule”). But the Hiphil makes no sense with “kings” as object; one must understand an ellipsis and supply “him” (Cyrus) as the object. The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has יוֹרִיד (yorid), which appears to be a Hiphil form from יָרַד (yarad, “go down”). Others suggest reading יָרֹד (yarod), a Qal form from רָדַד (radad, “beat down”).

*Study note:* The point is that they are powerless before Cyrus’ military power and scatter before him.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[in] peace”; KJV, ASV “safely”; NASB “in safety”; NIV “unscathed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a way with his feet he does not come [or “enter”].” One could translate, “by a way he was not [previously] entering with his feet.” This would mean that he is advancing into new territory and expanding his conquests. The present translation assumes this is a hyperbolic description of his speedy advance. He moves so quickly he does not enter the way with his feet, i.e., his feet don’t even touch the ground. See C. R. North, *Second Isaiah*, 94.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Who acts and accomplishes?”; NASB “Who has performed and accomplished it.”

*Translator's note:* The interrogative particle is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I, the Lord, [am with] the first, and with the last ones I [am] he.”

*Translator's note:* Or “islands” (NIV, CEV); NCV “faraway places”; NLT “lands beyond the sea.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the ends of the earth,” but this is a merism, where the earth’s extremities stand for its entirety, i.e., the extremities and everything in between them.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “each his neighbor helps”; NCV “The workers help each other.”

*Translator's note:* The verb “encourages” is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “saying of the welding, ‘It is good.’”
*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “covenantal partner” (see 1 Kgs 5:15 HT [{{1 Kings 5:1|5:1}} ET]; 2 Chr 20:7).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “whom I have taken hold of [i.e., to lead back].”

*Translator's note:* According to BDB (1043 s.v. שָׁעָה), the verb תִּשְׁתָּע (tishtaʿ) in the second line of the poetic couplet is a Hitpael form from the root שָׁעָה (shaʿah, “gaze,” with metathesis of the stem prefix and the first root letter). Taking the Hitpael as iterative, one may then translate “do not anxiously look about.” However, the alleged Hitpael form of שָׁעָה (shaʿah) only occurs here and in verse {{Isaiah 41:23|23}}. *HALOT* 1671 s.v. שׁתע proposes that the verb is instead a Qal form from the root שׁתע (“fear”). Its attestation in cognate Semitic languages, including Ugaritic (discovered after the publishing of BDB), suggests the existence of this root. The poetic structure of v. {{Isaiah 41:10|10}} also supports the proposal, for the form in question is in synonymous parallelism to יָרֵא (yareʾ, “fear”).

*Translator's note:* The “right hand” is a symbol of the Lord’s power to deliver ({{Exodus 15:6|Exod 15:6}}, {{Exodus 15:12|12}}) and protect (Ps 63:9 HT [{{Psalm 63:8|63:8}} ET]). Here צֶדֶק (tsedeq) has its well-attested nuance of “vindicated righteousness,” i.e., “victory, deliverance” (see {{Isaiah 45:8|45:8}}; {{Isaiah 51:5|51:5}}, and BDB 841-42 s.v.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the men of your strife”; NASB “those who contend with you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like nothing”; NAB “come to nought.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the men of your struggle”; NASB “those who quarrel with you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the men of your battle”; NAB “who do battle with you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O worm Jacob” (NAB, NIV84); NIV11 “you worm Jacob.” The worm metaphor suggests that Jacob is insignificant and despised.

*Translator's note:* On the basis of the parallelism (note “worm”) and an alleged Akkadian cognate, some read “louse” or “weevil.” Cf. NAB “O maggot Israel”; NRSV “you insect Israel.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your kinsman redeemer.” A גֹּאֵל (goʾel, “kinsman redeemer”) was a protector of the extended family’s interests.

*Study note:* See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in {{Isaiah 1:4|1:4}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “into” (so NIV); ASV “have made thee to be.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “owner of two-mouths,” i.e., double-edged.

*Study note:* The mountains and hills symbolize hostile nations that are obstacles to Israel’s restoration.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will answer them” (so ASV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

*Study note:* The rift valley (עֲרָבָה, ʿaravah) is known for its arid, desert-like conditions in the area of the Dead Sea and southward (although it also includes the Jordan Valley, extending from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba). The point here is the contrast from its normal arid conditions to being productive with trees, which implies being watered. Similarly, the wilderness (מִדְבָּר, midbar) in the first line is an area that receives less than twelve inches of rainfall annually and so cannot support trees.

*Translator's note:* The words “I will do this” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The Hebrew text has here simply, “in order that.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they”; NAB, NRSV “that all may see”; CEV, NLT “Everyone will see.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hand” (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* Or “created it” (KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV); TEV “has made it happen.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “strong [words],” see *HALOT* 870 s.v. *עֲצֻמוֹת.

*Study note:* Apparently this challenge is addressed to the pagan idol gods, see vv. {{Isaiah 41:23|23-24}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “As for the former things, tell us what they are!”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so we might set [them to] our heart.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and might know their outcome.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Declare the coming things, with respect to the end.”

*Text-critical note:* The translation assumes the *Qere* (וְנִרְאֶה [venirʾeh], from יָרֵא [yareʾ], “be afraid”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so we might be frightened and afraid together.” On the meaning of the verb שָׁתָע (shataʿ), see the note at v. {{Isaiah 41:10|10}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “an object of disgust [is he who] chooses you.”

*Study note:* That is, Cyrus the Persian. See the note at v. {{Isaiah 41:2|2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[one] from the rising of the sun [who] calls in my name.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has וְיָבֹא (veyavoʾ, “and he comes”), but this likely needs to be emended to an original וַיָּבָס (vayyavas), from בּוּס (bus, “step on”).
*Translator's note:* The words “who announced it” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The interrogative particle and verb are understood by ellipsis (see the preceding line).
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads simply, “First to Zion, ‘Look here they are!’” The words “I decreed” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text has אָוֶן (ʾaven, “deception,” i.e., “false”), but the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has אין (“nothing”), which forms a better parallel with אֶפֶס (ʾefes, “nothing”) in the next line. See also {{Isaiah 40:17|40:17}} and {{Isaiah 41:12|41:12}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their statues are wind and nothing”; NASB “wind and emptiness”; NIV “wind and confusion.”

*Study note:* Verses {{Isaiah 42:1|1-7}} contain the first of Isaiah’s “servant songs,” which describe the ministry of a special, ideal servant who accomplishes God’s purposes for Israel and the nations. This song depicts the servant as a just king who brings justice to the earth and relief for the oppressed. The other songs appear in {{Isaiah 49:1|49:1-13}}; {{Isaiah 50:4|50:4-11}}; and {{Isaiah 52:13|52:13-53:12}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he will bring out justice” (cf. ASV, NASB, NRSV).

*Study note:* Like the ideal king portrayed in {{Isaiah 11:1|Isa 11:1-9}}, the servant is energized by the divine spirit and establishes justice on the earth.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he will not cause his voice to be heard in the street.”

*Study note:* The “crushed reed” and “dim wick” symbolize the weak and oppressed who are on the verge of extinction.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “faithfully he will bring out justice” (cf. NASB, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* For rhetorical effect the terms used to describe the “crushed (רָצַץ, ratsats) reed” and “dim (כָּהָה, kahah) wick” in v. {{Isaiah 42:3|3}} are repeated here.

*Translator's note:* Or “islands” (NIV); NLT “distant lands beyond the sea.”

*Translator's note:* Or “his law” (KJV, ASV, NASB, NIV84) or “his instruction” (NLT) or “his teaching” (NIV11).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the God.” The definite article here indicates distinctiveness or uniqueness.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and its offspring” (so NASB); NIV84 “all that comes out of it”; NIV11 “all that springs from it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and spirit [i.e., “breath”] to the ones walking in it” (NAB, NASB, and NRSV all similar).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “call you in righteousness.” The pronoun “you” is masculine singular, referring to the servant. See the note at {{Isaiah 41:2|41:2}}.

*Translator's note:* The translation assumes the verb is derived from the root נָצַר (natsar, “protect”). Some prefer to derive it from the root יָצַר (yatsar, “form”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a covenant of people.” A person cannot literally be a covenant; בְּרִית (berit) is probably metonymic here, indicating a covenant mediator. The precise identity of עָם (ʿam, “people”) is uncertain. In v. {{Isaiah 42:5|5}} עָם refers to mankind, and the following reference to “nations” also favors this. But in {{Isaiah 49:8|49:8}}, where the phrase בְּרִית עָם occurs again, Israel seems to be in view.

*Study note:* Light here symbolizes deliverance from bondage and oppression; note the parallelism in {{Isaiah 49:6|49:6b}} and in {{Isaiah 51:4|51:4-6}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “the Gentiles” (so KJV, ASV, NIV); the same Hebrew word can be translated “nations” or “Gentiles” depending on the context.

*Study note:* This does not refer to literal physical healing of the blind. As the next two lines suggest, this refers metonymically to freeing captives from their dark prisons where their eyes have grown unaccustomed to light.

*Study note:* This does not refer to hardened, dangerous criminals, who would have been executed for their crimes in ancient Near Eastern society. This verse refers to political prisoners or victims of social injustice.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the former things, look, they have come.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “before they sprout up, I cause you to hear.” The pronoun “you” is plural, referring to the people of Israel. In this verse “the former things” are the Lord’s earlier predictive oracles which have come to pass, while “the new things” are predicted events that have not yet begun to take place. “The former things” are earlier events in Israel’s history which God announced beforehand, such as the Exodus (see {{Isaiah 43:16|43:16-18}}). “The new things” are the predictions about the servant ({{Isaiah 42:1|42:1-7}}). and may also include Cyrus’ conquests ({{Isaiah 41:25|41:25-27}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his praise.” The phrase stands parallel to “new song” in the previous line.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and its fullness”; NASB, NIV “and all that is in it.”

*Translator's note:* Or “islands” (NASB, NIV); NLT “distant coastlands.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Let them ascribe to the Lord glory.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and his praise in the coastlands [or “islands”] let them declare.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like a man of war he stirs up zeal” (NIV similar).

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “he triumphs over his enemies” (cf. NIV); NLT “will crush all his enemies.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “silent” (so NASB, NIV, TEV, NLT); CEV “have held my temper.”

*Study note:* The imagery depicts the Lord as a warrior who is eager to fight and can no longer hold himself back from the attack.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will dry up the mountains and hills.” The “mountains and hills” stand by synecdoche for the trees that grow on them. Some prefer to derive the verb from a homonymic root and translate, “I will lay waste.”

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text reads, “I will turn streams into coastlands [or “islands”].” Scholars who believe that this reading makes little sense have proposed an emendation of אִיִּים (ʾiyyim, “islands”) to צִיּוֹת (tsiyyot, “dry places”; cf. NCV, NLT, TEV). However, since all the versions support the MT reading, there is insufficient grounds for an emendation here. Although the imagery of changing rivers into islands is somewhat strange, J. N. Oswalt describes this imagery against the backdrop of rivers of the Near East. The receding of these rivers at times occasioned the appearance of previously submerged islands (*Isaiah* [NICOT], 2:126).

*Study note:* The imagery of this verse, which depicts the Lord bringing a curse of infertility to the earth, metaphorically describes how the Lord will destroy his enemies.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a way they do not know” (so NASB); NRSV “a road they do not know.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in paths they do not know I will make them walk.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the rough ground into a level place.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “be ashamed with shame”; ASV, NASB “be utterly put to shame.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “look to see”; NAB, NCV “look and see”; NRSV “look up and see.”

*Text-critical note:* The precise meaning of מְשֻׁלָּם (meshullam) in this context is uncertain. In later biblical Hebrew the form (which appears to be a Pual participle from the root שָׁלַם, shalam) occurs as a proper name, Meshullam. The Pual of שָׁלַם (“be complete”) is attested with the meaning “repaid, requited,” but that makes little sense here. BDB 1023 s.v. שָׁלַם relates the form to the denominative verb שָׁלַם (“be at peace”) and paraphrases “one in a covenant of peace” (J. N. Oswalt suggests “the covenanted one”; *Isaiah* [NICOT], 2:128, n. 59) Some emend the form to מֹשְׁלָם (moshelam, “their ruler”) or to מְשֻׁלָּחִי (meshullakhi, “my sent [or “commissioned”] one”), which fits nicely in the parallelism (note “my messenger” in the previous line). The translation above assumes an emendation to כְּמוֹ שֹׁלְמִי (kemo sholemi, “like my ally”). Isaiah uses כְּמוֹ in {{Isaiah 30:22|30:22}} and perhaps {{Isaiah 51:5|51:5}}; for שֹׁלְמי (“my ally”) see Ps 7:5 HT ({{Psalm 7:4|7:4}} ET).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Who is blind but my servant, and deaf like my messenger I send? Who is blind like my commissioned one, blind like the servant of the Lord?” The point of the rhetorical questions is that no one is as blind/deaf as this servant. In this context the Lord’s “servant” is exiled Israel (cf. {{Isaiah 41:8|41:8-9}}), which is spiritually blind and deaf and has failed to fulfill God’s purpose for it. This servant stands in contrast to the ideal “Israel” of the servant songs.

*Translator's note:* The consonantal text (*Kethib*) has a perfect, second person masculine singular; the marginal reading (*Qere*) has an infinitive absolute, which functions here as a finite verb.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but you do not guard [i.e., retain in your memory]”; NIV11 “but you pay no attention.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “The Lord was pleased for the sake of his righteousness [or “justice”], he was magnifying [the] law and was making [it] glorious.” The Lord contrasts his good intentions for the people with their present crisis (v. {{Isaiah 42:22|22}}). To demonstrate his just character and attract the nations, the Lord wanted to showcase his law among and through Israel ({{Deuteronomy 4:5|Deut 4:5-8}}). But Israel disobeyed (v. {{Isaiah 42:24|24}}) and failed to carry out their commission.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text has בַּחוּרִים (bakhurim, “young men”), but the text should be emended to בְּהוֹרִים (behorim, “in holes”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and made to be hidden”; NAB, NASB, NIV, TEV “hidden away in prisons.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they became loot, and there was no one rescuing, plunder, and there was no one saying, ‘Bring back’.”
*Translator's note:* The interrogative particle is understood in the second line by ellipsis (note the preceding line).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Who gave to the robber Jacob, and Israel to the looters?” In the first line the consonantal text (*Kethib*) has מְשׁוֹסֶה (meshoseh), a Polel participle from שָׁסָה (shasah, “plunder”). The marginal reading (*Qere*) is מְשִׁיסָּה (meshissah), a noun meaning “plunder.” In this case one could translate “Who handed Jacob over as plunder?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they were not willing in his ways to walk, and they did not listen to his law.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew third masculine singular pronoun, representing the nation, has been rendered as the third plural throughout this verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “strength” (so KJV, NASB); NAB “fury”; NASB “fierceness”; NIV “violence.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and it blazed against him all around.” The subject of the third feminine singular verb “blazed” is the divine חֵמָה (khemah, “anger”) mentioned in the previous line.

*Study note:* It is not that he did not know about the war, but he did not attribute this to God’s wrath.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but he did not set [it] upon [his] heart.” The Hebrew word “heart” also refers to the mind.
*Translator's note:* Or “redeem.” See the note at {{Isaiah 41:14|41:14}}. Cf. NCV “saved you”; CEV “rescued you”; NLT “ransomed you.”

*Translator's note:* The verb is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “burn” (so NASB); NAB, NRSV, NLT “consume”; NIV “set you ablaze.”

*Study note:* See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in {{Isaiah 1:4|1:4}}.

*Study note:* *Seba* is not the same as Sheba in southern Arabia; cf. {{Genesis 1:10|Gen 1:10}}; 1 Chr 1:9.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Since you are precious in my eyes and you are honored.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “everyone who is called by my name” (so NASB, NIV, NRSV).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the former things he was causing us to hear?”

*Translator's note:* Or “know” (KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and after me, there will not be”; NASB “there will be none after Me.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hand” (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV); NLT “No one can oppose what I do.”

*Translator's note:* Or “kinsman redeemer.” See the note at {{Isaiah 41:14|41:14}}.

*Study note:* See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in {{Isaiah 1:4|1:4}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I bring down [as] fugitives all of them.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “as for the Babylonians, in ships their joyful shout.” This might be paraphrased, “even the Babylonians in the ships [over which] they joyfully shouted.” The point would be that the Lord caused the Babylonians to flee for safety in the ships in which they took such great pride. A slight change in vocalization yields the reading “into mourning songs,” which provides a good contrast with “joyful shout.” The prefixed bet (בְּ) would indicate identity.
*Study note:* See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in {{Isaiah 1:4|1:4}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “led out chariots and horses.” The words “to destruction” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The verse refers to the destruction of the Egyptians at the Red Sea.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lay down”; NAB “lie prostrate together”; CEV “lie dead”; NRSV “they lie down.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the former things” (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV); NLT “forget all that.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sprouts up”; NASB “will spring forth.”

*Translator's note:* Or “know” (KJV, ASV); NASB “be aware of”; NAB, NIV, NRSV “perceive.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has “streams,” probably under the influence of v. {{Isaiah 43:20|20}}. The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has נתיבות (“paths”).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[so] they might declare my praise.”
*Translator's note:* Or “strive”; KJV, ASV, NRSV “been weary of me.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with.” The words “by demanding” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* That is, “calamus” (so NIV); NCV, TEV, NLT “incense”; CEV “spices.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you did not saturate me”; NASB “Neither have you filled Me.”

*Study note:* In vv. {{Isaiah 43:22|22-24}} the Lord appears to be condemning his people for failure to bring the proper sacrifices. However, this is problematic. If this refers to the nation’s behavior while in exile, such cultic service was impossible and could hardly be expected by the Lord. If this refers to the nation’s conduct before the exile, it contradicts other passages that depict Israel as bringing excessive sacrifices (see, e.g., {{Isaiah 1:11|Isa 1:11-14}}; Jer 6:20; {{Amos 4:4|Amos 4:4-5}}; {{Isaiah 5:21|5:21-23}}). Rather than being a condemnation of Israel’s failure to bring sacrifices, these verses are better taken as a highly rhetorical comment on the worthlessness of Israel’s religious ritual. They may have brought sacrifices, but not to the Lord, for he did not accept them or even want them. See C. R. North, *Second Isaiah*, 127, and R. Whybray, *{{Isaiah 40|Isaiah 40-66}}* (NCBC), 91.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you, tell in order that you may be right”; NAB “prove your innocence.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your first father.” This could refer to Abraham (see {{Isaiah 51:2|51:2}}), but elsewhere in Isaiah he does not appear in a negative light (see {{Isaiah 29:22|29:22}}; {{Isaiah 41:8|41:8}}; {{Isaiah 63:16|63:16}}). A more likely candidate is Jacob/Israel, also referred to as the nation’s “father” elsewhere (see {{Isaiah 58:14|58:14}}; {{Isaiah 63:16|63:16}}).

*Translator's note:* On the meaning of the term לִיץ (lits), see *HALOT* 590 s.v. מֵלִיץ. This may refer to the nation’s prophets, priests, and/or kings.
*Translator's note:* The word “subjected” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
*Study note:* *Jeshurun* is a poetic name for Israel; it occurs here and in {{Deuteronomy 32:15|Deut 32:15}}; {{Deuteronomy 33:5|33:5}}, {{Deuteronomy 33:26|26}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the thirsty.” Parallelism suggests that dry ground is in view (see “dry land” in the next line.)

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and streams”; KJV “floods.” The verb “cause…to flow” is supplied in the second line for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term בֵין (ven) is usually taken as a preposition, in which case one might translate, “among the grass.” But בֵין is probably the name of a tree (cf. C. R. North, *Second Isaiah*, 133). If one alters the preposition bet (בְּ) to kaf (כְּ), one can then read, “like a binu-tree.” (The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa supports this reading.) This forms a nice parallel to “like poplars” in the next line. חָצִיר (khatsir) is functioning as an adverbial accusative of location.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has a Qal verb form, “and another will call by the name of Jacob.” With support from Symmachus (an ancient Greek textual witness), some read the Niphal, “and another will be called by the name of Jacob.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and by the name of Israel he will title.” Some, with support from several ancient versions, prefer to change the Piel (active) verb form to a Pual (passive), “and he will be titled by the name of Israel.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his kinsman redeemer.” See the note at {{Isaiah 41:14|41:14}}.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text reads, “from (the time) I established an ancient people, and the coming things.” Various emendations have been proposed.
